status: Proposed real explanation/assessment correction; downstream compatibility review required

before.description: Understand what bullying is — repeated behaviour intended to hurt someone, including physical, verbal, social (exclusion, spreading rumours), and cyberbullying — and know that it is always wrong and what to do if they experience or witness it
before.evidence0: Define bullying and distinguish it from a one-off conflict

after.description: Recognise bullying in the applicable school or community context: harmful aggression involving a real or perceived power imbalance, commonly repeated, including physical, verbal, social and online forms. Distinguish bullying from an ordinary disagreement, recognise that definitions and context matter, and know how to seek help for harmful behaviour without waiting for it to repeat or proving another person’s intention.
after.evidence0: Use a stated school or community definition to distinguish bullying from an ordinary disagreement, considering harm, power and the pattern or context; explain that a single harmful incident can still require help even if its label is uncertain.

wholeOperationWitnesses.oldPassNewMissing: A learner names physical/verbal/social/cyber forms and help steps for repeated intentional aggression but says one serious power-imbalanced harmful online posting cannot count, or no help is needed without admission of intent. The older task may pass while the revised context/power distinction fails.
wholeOperationWitnesses.positive: Given a clearly stated local definition and illustrated facts, distinguish a disagreement between peers able to express views from targeted harmful aggression involving unequal power; explain safe reporting and why repetition or proven intention is not a precondition for help.
wholeOperationWitnesses.nearMiss: Every argument is bullying, one incident can never be bullying, the target must prove intent, or the safest action is to confront the aggressor alone.
wholeOperationWitnesses.transfer: Change from repeated exclusion to a single widely circulated harmful impersonation in a stated school context; retain power/context reasoning and seek support even if a legal classification is not yet certain.

Ontario.interpretation: The provincial public guidance can include a single event; policy uses typically repeated aggression and real/perceived power imbalance, with intentional or reasonably foreseeable harm. Apply the actual school/community context rather than silently substitute a global repetition/intent rule.

Australia.interpretation: The Australian national school frame requires deliberate harm, misuse of power and repetition or potential repetition. One online sharing action can satisfy the pattern condition through continuing circulation; a one-off equal-power conflict does not. This frame is retained rather than declared wrong.

boundaries: No claim that one jurisdiction supplies the universal legal definition. Use the actually applicable school/community frame and ordinary reasoned distinctions.
A one-off harm report does not automatically certify that an incident legally constitutes bullying.
No manufactured bullying, threats, private victim history, graphic images, slurs or unsafe confrontation.
No delay in help because an incident is isolated, the child is calm or an actor denies intending harm.
Keep old three-form inventory, help steps, assessment prompt, contexts and dependencies exact except the two proposed paths.
compatibility: Real explanatory/assessment criterion revision, not wording-only. Old claim revision must remain available downstream; no automatic mastery equivalence, learner reset or evidence transfer.
preservation: Only description and evidence[0] change. Stable ID, name, other evidence, assessmentPrompt, every old source/age context and all five affected edges remain exact. No guide exists and none is added.
resourceReadback: Actual Ontario public main body and PPM definition section captured/read; actual Australian main article and full published definition transcripts read. Dates/source interpretation are not intervention-efficacy claims.
